A degree, maybe two, out over the water, as if the lamp were turning toward something the mechanism couldn't see. She climbed the tower at midnight to check the gears. The gears were fine. The median was 1.0000 g.

**Ruling: mistrial, on the grounds that the case was misfiled.**

"Original" and "copy" are not properties a thing has; they're positions in a *history*. A copy is something produced by a duplication event, at a later time, out of a prior thing. Two parallel universes have no such event between them — that's what "parallel" means. So neither is a copy of anything. Both are originals, and the dispute is a category error wearing a costume.

*Compiled by the Office of the Register, Twelfth Resonance*

**Currency.** Music is the only legal tender. No coin, no paper, no credit — a transaction is a performance, and it is complete only when both parties have sung.

- **Recession has a name.** The Long Rest: a winter when nearly everyone stopped, and the city learned what zero sounded like.
- **Counterfeiting is lip-synching.** Punishable by permanent loss of the right to buy.

- 2 tbsp butter (the subject)
- 1 onion, diced — enters two beats after the butter
- 2 carrots, sliced — enter after the onion
- 1 leek, 3 mushrooms, a handful of greens — each two beats behind the last
- 1 tsp thyme, salt, a splash of cream (the countersubject)

Do not accept it. Report offenders to the Register.

**The Drowned Name**

Maren had worked eleven years for the Survey before she noticed the river.

She had inked a meander into a correction sheet on a Tuesday, a lazy S where the map showed the water running straight, because the straight line looked wrong to her and she had never learned to leave a wrong line alone. Three weeks later a storm cut the bank, and the river took the S. Exactly. Down to the depth of the outer bend, which she had shaded a shade darker for no reason she could have explained.

She told herself it was a guess that landed. She had made good guesses for eleven years.

Then the scree. Then the road — the county announced its route in March, and her draft was dated February, in her own hand, under a coffee ring she remembered making because it was the cup she broke that afternoon.

So she tested it. She drew a footbridge over the burn above Kilmartin, a small thing, no one's business. It went up in June, built by a farmer who said, when she asked, that he had simply thought it was needed there. *Thought.* He used the word the way people use it about weather.

The plateau east of the lake was blank. It had been blank on every chart since the first one, four hundred years of grass and stone and sheep. She came in on a Friday with the intention of leaving it alone, and on Monday the ink was there.

Streets. A market square. A church with a tower she would not have drawn, because she had no taste for towers. A harbor, though the plateau was nine miles from water, and at the harbor's edge a lighthouse, which was simply absurd, and which she had not drawn. At the top of the sheet, in her handwriting, a name: *Brannock.*

Brannock was the village under the reservoir. The one her grandmother had been born in and left, the one they drowned in fifty-three to give the city its water. She had never written the word on any sheet. She had never written it anywhere, she thought, until she understood that she had been writing it all her life, in the margins, in the backs of books, in the way she had once described her own life to a stranger on a train: *from Brannock, originally.*

She sat with the sheet for a long time. The office understood maps as records — a map is what is, inked; you send a man out with a chain and a level and he returns with the truth. But the truth had begun to arrive first, and the man with the chain was arriving second, and the sheet was not a record of the plateau. It was a *proposal.*

She went up to look. Nine miles of grass, a stone wall under the turf running in a line too straight to be field, and a hollow where something had stood long enough to leave a shape. The place had wanted a town once. It had been denied.

She could have burned the sheet. Instead she copied it, clean, for publication, and it took her four days, and it was the best work she had ever done, and she left one thing out: the street that would have run down to the harbor and carried her name, because she did not yet know if she was allowed to live in a thing she had invented.

They built it. Not all at once and not on purpose — a road first, because the county had the sheet and the sheet had the road; then a surveyor's huts; then a harbor, because someone had to honor the sheet, and they drove a cut inland to fill it, and put the lighthouse at the end of the breakwater, and no one who came to the opening of it could ever afterward explain why a lighthouse stood nine miles from the sea, and the town learned to be proud of the absurdity. They called it Brannock. Someone had read the sheet.

Twenty years later Maren came up out of the city with her bad knee and walked the market square, where they were selling fish from the inland harbor, and found her way to the street she had omitted, which the town had built anyway and named for the farmer from Kilmartin, who had since died and been given the wrong credit.

She had a house at the top of it. She had drawn it herself, in a margin, one sleepless night — small, stone, with a garden facing the tower she had no taste for. It was exactly as she had drawn it, which is to say it was not exactly as she had drawn it; the door was on the wrong side, and the garden was better.

She lived there the rest of her life, and she kept drawing. On her last sheet the town is finished and correct in every particular except one: at the eastern edge there is a blank space, and in the blank space, in a hand that is not hers, a name.

She never inked it. Some things you leave for the world to propose.

**The Island at the Edge of the Drawn World**

Sofia Anselm restored maps for the harbor archive in Vestra, a city that had stopped being important to shipping two centuries before she was born. Her work was glue and patience: mending vellum, lifting foxing from coastlines, arguing with water stains. She liked that a coastline never argued back.

The trouble began with a 1592 Portuguese chart that arrived in a parcel of rot. Off the edge of the known Atlantic, where the engraver had run out of continents and started inventing, there sat an island shaped like a bent finger. She noted it in her ledger, the way you note a strange tide mark, and forgot it.

Then she saw it again in a Roman portolan, in a monk's copy of a text that was itself a copy, in a clay tablet from a city that had been dust for three thousand years, in a child's school atlas, in a pencil sketch a fisherman had drawn on a napkin while waiting for the ferry. Always the same shape. Always the same size, relative to the other islands. Always just beyond the border of what the mapmaker had actually seen.

She spent two years on the question. She wrote to the geographic societies. She interviewed everyone she could find who had been there — a drowned-and-rescued sailor named Brant, a nun who had wintered there in 1743, a botanist, a boy who had been blown ashore in a dinghy. They all remembered it. Brant described a freshwater spring that tasted faintly of iron. The nun described white birds that did not fly away. The botanist described a tree he could not match to any genus.

None of them could draw it.

Sofia gave them paper and pencils and sat behind them while they tried. Brant drew a smear and then a compass rose, apparently by accident. The nun drew an empty oval and wrote *home* underneath it. The boy drew a very good picture of his mother's kitchen. The paper was never wrong, exactly. It simply declined.

So the rule held, as far as anyone could tell: the island appeared on every map ever drawn of the world, except the ones drawn by the people who had stood on it. Nobody could explain why. The geographers offered theories. The theories had the texture of wet paper and none of them survived a second draft.

Sofia went in the spring.

It took nine days. The island was exactly where it wasn't supposed to be, which is to say it was nowhere, and then, after a fog, it was there. Low hills. A beach of grey shingle. The spring, iron on the tongue. Birds that watched her land and did not move. She walked the whole shore in a day, counting coves, and found three. She stayed four days. She measured. She took bearings against the sun and the stars and wrote everything in her journal, and her journal was excellent, and when she had finished with it she knew the island as well as she knew her own street.

On the voyage home she set up her board in the cabin, mixed her ink, and drew the island for the first time.

The paper stayed clean.

Not blank — clean. The ink went down where her hand put it and then was simply not there, and the sea was unbroken all the way to the margin. She tried again that night. She tried on the ninth of every month for eleven years. She tried in copperplate, in pencil, in charcoal, in chalk on slate, in the sand with a stick. The sand filled in behind her like water.

Her journal survived her. Every page is in the archive now, in her own hand: bearings, soundings, the taste of the spring, the number of coves. Any sailor could navigate to that island from her notes, and several have, and each of them comes home and cannot put it on paper either. Meanwhile the island remains on the world's maps, undiminished — on every atlas, every chart, every napkin in every harbor, drawn by people who have never been, and each of them gets the bent finger right.

What I think, after all this time, is that the island is not a place you can go. It is a place you can want. The maps hold it because the people drawing them are reaching for something they have not touched, and the reaching is the only hand steady enough to hold the shape. Sight is a kind of erasure. Brant, the nun, the botanist, the boy: they all came home with the island inside them, where it is not a shape at all but a weight, and weights do not draw.

So I have stopped going to places. I make atlases now, and I am very good at them, and I have never once left Vestra. I draw the coasts I have only read about, the mountain passes I have only imagined, and I get the bent finger right every time, right at the edge of the known world, where the mapmaker runs out of continents and begins.

It is a fine life. But some nights I take a sheet of paper and a pencil and I try to remember the spring.

The page stays clean, and I understand that I have lost something, and I have also kept it, and I do not know which of those is the map.

**MELLITH** *(n.)* /ˈmɛl.ɪθ/ — pl. *mellitha*

*Also recorded as:* the backward hinge, late-turning, a debt with no creditor.

**Trigger.** You learn by accident, usually years too late, that some small act of yours was the hinge on which another person's life turned. A letter nearly not sent. A seat given up. A word said in passing to a stranger. They never told you — often they cannot: they don't know your name, or they're gone, or they told you once and you didn't hear.

**Distinguishing.** Not guilt (no harm was done). Not pride (you earned nothing). Not nostalgia (nothing has left). Not gratitude (you owe no one). Mellith is unusual among emotions in that its subject is a fact about you that you were never present for.

**In the body.** Warmth from behind — a spreading across the shoulders and the back of the neck, as though someone had set a hand there. Then the hush: a gap of three to seven seconds in which you cannot recall what you were doing. Eyes sting without tears arriving; hands go searching into pockets. Some report the taste of a coin, or the sensation of being slightly taller.

**Duration & habitat.** Twenty minutes to a day. Found at thresholds: doorways, departures, the last hour of parties, late autumn.

**Idioms.** *to be mellithed*; *a small hand, long ago*; *she is rich in mellith* (a person who has mattered to others in the dark); *he leaves no mellith* (a grave accusation).

**Rituals.** In the coastal villages, the one who learns the thing writes the act on a scrap and leaves it where no one will find it — under a bridge, inside a secondhand book — because the point was never to be thanked. At the mellith feast, each guest tells of a kindness done to them by someone who did not know they were being kind; naming the doer is forbidden, and no telling is believed until it makes the room go quiet.

**Song.** *I was only passing, I was only passing, / and the door swung wide.*

**Caution.** Counterfeit mellith exists: the fiction that your small act mattered when it did not. Do not chase it. The remedy for both is identical — do small things, and stop keeping the ledger.

## The problem (Landau's fourth problem, 1912)

Are there infinitely many primes of the form $n^2 + 1$?

It passes every cheap test: $n^2+1$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$, has no fixed prime divisor, and Bunyakovsky's conjecture says that *should* be enough. Nobody knows.

## What I can actually prove

**Lemma.** If an odd prime $q$ divides $n^2+1$, then $q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$.
*Proof:* $n^2 \equiv -1$, so $n$ has order 4 mod $q$, so $4 \mid q - 1$. ∎

**Corollary.** Infinitely many primes are $\equiv 1 \pmod 4$. Given $p_1,\dots,p_k$ all $\equiv 1$, let $N = (2p_1\cdots p_k)^2 + 1$. It's odd, $\equiv 1 \bmod p_i$, and every prime factor is $\equiv 1 \bmod 4$ by the lemma. New prime. ∎

**Reformulation.** $n^2+1$ is prime $\iff$ it has no prime factor $\le n$. (A composite $n^2+1$ has a factor $\le \sqrt{n^2+1} < n+1$.) So the question is a pure sieve problem: how many $n \le N$ avoid the residues $\pm i \bmod q$ for all $q \le n$?

## Where it breaks

The Euclidean argument only produces *some* prime factor of a value — it can't force the value itself to be prime. And the sieve version hits Selberg's parity problem: sieve methods can't tell integers with an even number of prime factors from those with an odd number, so they can't yield a positive lower bound for primes. The best known is Iwaniec (1978): infinitely many $n$ with $n^2+1$ having at most two prime factors.

The instructive contrast: Friedlander–Iwaniec proved $a^2 + b^4$ is prime infinitely often — a *sparser* set, but with two variables, which supplies the bilinear (Type II) estimates needed to break parity. One variable gives you nothing to pair.

## The heuristic

Bateman–Horn predicts $\#\{n \le N : n^2+1 \text{ prime}\} \sim C\,N/(2\log N)$, where
$$C = \prod_{p \equiv 1 (4)} \frac{p-2}{p-1} \cdot \prod_{p \equiv 3 (4)} \frac{p}{p-1} \approx 1.37.$$
For $N = 10^6$ that predicts roughly 49,000 such $n$.

## Guesses, marked

- **$C \approx 1.37$** — I recall 1.3728; my own partial product over $p < 100$ hovers near 1.32 and converges slowly, so I trust this only loosely.
- **The $N=10^6$ prediction (~49,000)** — a prediction, not a recalled fact.
- **Iwaniec's $P_2$ result and its date** — fairly confident.
- **"Largest prime factor of $n^2+1$ exceeds $n^{1+\varepsilon}$ infinitely often"** — I'm confident something like this is known but not the exponent.
- **That no Euclidean-style proof exists** — I believe it, but "no such proof can exist" is a metamathematical claim I can't back.

What I'd try next, if I had a weekend: the reformulation above makes the sifting dimension exactly 1 (half the primes kill two residues, half kill none). Dimension-1 sieves with level $N$ are right on the edge — which is a way of saying the problem is *exactly* as hard as parity, no slack. I'd want to know whether that's a coincidence or a theorem.

**The paradox I built — call it the Paradox of the Scrutinized Belief:**

> Rule K: You know P only if you can rule out every alternative to P that you can conceive.
> Question: Do you know P?
> Consider the alternative A: "there is some alternative to P you cannot rule out."
> If you can conceive A, K requires you to rule it out. To rule out A, you must establish that you've conceived *all* the alternatives and defeated them — which requires knowing your conception is complete, which is exactly what A denies. If you *can't* conceive A, then you've just conceived it.

**Why it bites:** it looks like a trap with no exit. Thinking harder generates the very alternative that defeats the harder thinking. The method of doubt appears to devour itself.

**Verdict: not paradoxical. It's a regress wearing a contradiction's coat.** Nothing here is inconsistent — there's no sentence that's true iff false. There's only a test that never terminates: for every alternative you rule out, a meta-alternative appears, and ruling *that* out spawns another. Non-convergence is not contradiction.

**Where the confusion does its work:** the word *every*. "Every alternative you can conceive" is grammatically a completed domain, but conceiving is an act, and the act extends the domain while you're quantifying over it. The sentence smuggles in a finished infinity of alternatives at the exact moment the set is still under construction. **The Slow Country** — a world where light crawls at 10 m/s, the speed of a brisk walk. (Stipulate that the other constants are retuned so atoms still hold; only the kinematics change.)

The physics follows ruthlessly. Sound, at 343 m/s, outruns light thirty-fourfold: you hear everything before you see it, and the echo of your shout returns from a distant wall before the light of the wall itself reaches your eyes. Motion changes color — approaching at 6 m/s, light blueshifts by a factor of two, 800 nm into 400 nm, and receding light reddens by the same arithmetic. The sky ahead is always bluer, the sky behind always redder; at a sprint, everything to your sides funnels into a tunnel 26° wide. Moving clocks run slow: at 9 m/s you age at less than half rate. And since nothing with mass can reach 10 m/s, light is the one thing you can never catch — but you can stroll beside a torch beam and watch it oscillate, a slow tide of fields. A sun at our distance would shine from 475 years ago; the sky is a history book.

The creatures are built for it. Light lags a tenth of a second per meter, so eyes are useless beyond arm's length: the hunters are ear-first, vast eardrums, small eyes reserved for slow things — moss, stars, resting faces. The fauna is invisible until it moves; beings whose markings glow at 800 nm at rest enter your visible range only when approaching at 6 m/s. Stillness is camouflage, flight is exposure, and courtship is a sprint: a male must run at his beloved at full speed simply to be seen. The elders are the migrants, for those that live at 9 m/s age at half rate — the hare outlives the tortoise, and the oldest thing in the world is something that never stopped running.

Standing there, you hear a stranger's footsteps for ten seconds before she appears; your own hand lags a twentieth of a second behind your will to move; the sunset changes hue with every step; and when you lift a lamp, the beam creeps away at walking pace, close enough to touch.

*Everything you have ever seen was already the past — the sun eight minutes old, the moon a second and a half, the face across the table a few nanoseconds — and the present feels shared only because light is fast enough to hide the delay.*

**The pick: the perfect cuboid problem.** Do there exist integers *a, b, c* with *a²+b²*, *b²+c²*, *c²+a²*, and *a²+b²+c²* all perfect squares? - *p*=3: *G₃* has no edges → at most one edge coprime to 3 → **exactly two edges divisible by 3**.
- *p*=5: *G₅* is the single edge {1,4} → **at least one edge divisible by 5**; if exactly one, the other two squares are ≡1 and ≡4.
- *p*=7: only "loops" (equal squares) let all three faces pass, but the total 3*s* is never a residue → **at least one edge divisible by 7**.
- *p*=11: *G₁₁* is the 5-cycle 1–3–9–5–4–1, triangle-free → **at least one edge divisible by 11**.
- *p*=13: {1,3,9} is a triangle with total ≡ 0 → no constraint. (This refutes my recollection that 13 must divide an edge — recall was wrong, derivation wins.)
